description: Test your knowledge of Osteology: bone identification, vertebral anatomy, and pelvic dimensions.

cards.text: How do you identify a lumbar vertebra in anatomical position?
cards.answer: Large kidney-shaped vertebral body, short horizontal spinous process (hatchet-shaped pointing directly backward), slender transverse processes without costal facets, and vertical articular facets that face medially.

tip.tip: L = Large body, Lumbar = Locked (vertical facets prevent rotation)

cards.text: What is the clinical significance of the vertical orientation of lumbar articular facets?
cards.answer: Vertical orientation locks the lumbar vertebrae together, allowing flexion and extension while preventing rotation. This explains why lumbar rotation injuries are common causes of disc herniation.

tip.tip: Vertical facets = Flexion-extension only, no rotation

cards.text: In anatomical position, how is the sacrum oriented?
cards.answer: The concave pelvic surface faces anteriorly and inferiorly, the apex points inferiorly, and the sacral promontory (anterior upper border of S1) projects anteriorly.

cards.text: What is the difference between the true conjugate and obstetric conjugate diameters?
cards.answer: True conjugate (11 cm): promontory to inner surface of pubic symphysis, cannot be measured clinically. Obstetric conjugate (10.5 cm): smallest AP diameter, estimated clinically as diagonal conjugate minus 1.5 cm.

tip.tip: True = Not measurable clinically; Obstetric = Clinically estimated (diagonal − 1.5)

cards.text: How do you measure the diagonal conjugate clinically and why is it important?
cards.answer: The diagonal conjugate (12.5 cm) is measured per vaginum from the sacral promontory to the lower border of the pubic symphysis. It is clinically measurable and used to estimate the obstetric conjugate (diagonal − 1.5 cm).

tip.tip: Diagonal = Clinically measured; subtract 1.5 cm to estimate obstetric conjugate

cards.text: What are the boundaries of the pelvic inlet?
cards.answer: Anteriorly: upper border of pubic symphysis; Laterally: pectineal line and arcuate line of ilium; Posteriorly: sacral promontory.

tip.tip: Inlet = Triangle with promontory at back, pubic symphysis in front

cards.text: In anatomical position, what is the relationship between the ASIS, pubic symphysis, and pelvic tilt?
cards.answer: The anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) and upper edge of the pubic symphysis lie in the same vertical (coronal) plane, with the pelvic brim facing anterosuperiorly at approximately 60° to the horizontal.

tip.tip: ASIS & pubic symphysis = Same plane; Pelvic brim = 60° to horizontal

cards.text: What is the nutrient foramen and what principle guides its identification?
cards.answer: The nutrient foramen is an oblique opening in bone that transmits the nutrient artery. Its opening always faces AWAY from the growing end (epiphysis), which helps determine which end is proximal and which is distal.

tip.tip: Nutrient foramen = Opens AWAY from growth end (away from younger end)
